title: 📘 UNIT 9: THE AGE OF REVOLUTIONS, 1789 TO 1815
notes:
The Age of Revolutions → period of major political, economic, social and technological transformation.

Main revolutions/processes → Industrial Revolution + American War of Independence + French Revolution + Napoleonic Era.

title: 9.1 🏭 THE INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION
notes:
Industrial Revolution → greatly increased production of machine-made goods, beginning in England in the mid-18th century.

Traditional production → hand tools + household/workshop production.

Industrial production → machines + factories + wage labor.

Main industries transformed → textiles + iron + mechanical engineering + chemical manufacturing + transportation.

📌 Britain → first country where the Industrial Revolution developed on a large scale.

title: 9.1.1 🌾 Agricultural Revolution
notes:
Agricultural Revolution → major improvement in farming methods during the early 18th century.

Enclosure → large landowners fenced and consolidated land into larger farms.

Effects →
• Larger and more productive farms.
• Improved farming techniques.
• Increased food production.
• Population growth.
• Small farmers became tenants or moved to towns.
• Provided workers for factories.

🌱 Seed drill (c.1701) → allowed seeds to be planted at proper depth and spacing.

🔄 Crop rotation → improved soil use and increased agricultural productivity.

📌 Agricultural improvement helped create the food supply, population and labor force needed for industrialization.

title: 9.1.2 🇬🇧 Why Did the Industrial Revolution Begin in England?
notes:
Britain had several favorable conditions:

👥 Labor → growing population and available workers.

⛏️ Natural resources → coal + iron ore + water power.

🚢 Transportation → rivers + canals + harbors.

💰 Capital → wealthy business people invested in machines and factories.

🏦 Banking → developed banking system provided loans.

🌍 Trade → expanding overseas trade created markets and demand.

🏛️ Political stability → no major war was fought on British soil during the 18th century.

⚖️ Government → laws supported and protected business activities.

📌 Factors of production → land + labor + capital.

title: 9.1.3 🧵 Textile Revolution and Major Inventions
notes:
Textile industry → first major industry transformed by mechanization.

👤 John Kay → Flying Shuttle (1733) → increased weaving speed.

👤 James Hargreaves → Spinning Jenny (c.1764) → allowed one spinner to work several threads at once.

👤 Richard Arkwright → Water Frame (1769) → used water power for spinning.

👤 Samuel Crompton → Spinning Mule (1779) → produced stronger, finer and more consistent thread.

👤 Edmund Cartwright → Power Loom (1787) → greatly increased weaving speed.

👤 Eli Whitney → Cotton Gin (1793) → greatly increased the speed of removing seeds from cotton.

🏭 Factories → expensive machines moved spinning and weaving from homes into large centralized buildings.

title: 9.1.4 ⚙️ Steam Engine and Transportation
notes:
Steam power → provided a powerful source of mechanical energy for industry and transportation.

👤 James Watt → improved the steam engine in 1765, making it faster and more fuel-efficient.

🚢 Robert Fulton → steamboat Clermont made its first successful trip in 1807.

🛤️ Richard Trevithick → developed a steam-driven locomotive in 1804.

👤 George Stephenson → important early railway engineer; began work on a major railway line in 1821.

🚂 Effects of railways →
• Cheaper transportation of raw materials and products.
• Created jobs.
• Stimulated mining and industry.
• Expanded agricultural and fishing markets.
• Encouraged migration to cities.

title: 9.1.5 🏙️ Social and Economic Effects of Industrialization
notes:
Positive effects →
• Increased production.
• More employment.
• Economic growth.
• Technological progress.
• Higher wages for some workers.
• Cheaper mass-produced goods.
• Better housing and diets.
• Expanded education.
• Improved standard of living over time.

Negative effects →
• Long working hours.
• Dangerous factories and mines.
• Child labor.
• Air and water pollution.
• Poor working conditions.
• Urban overcrowding.
• Class inequality.
• Worker exploitation.

🏙️ Urbanization → rapid growth of cities as people moved from rural areas to industrial centers.

📌 Factory workers could work about 14 hours a day, 6 days a week during the early industrial period.

title: 9.1.6 👥 Class Tensions and the Luddites
notes:
Industrial society increasingly developed into:

🏦 Middle class/Bourgeoisie → factory owners + merchants + bankers + professionals + skilled workers.

👷 Working class/Proletariat → wage workers dependent on factory employment.

⚔️ Class tension → wealth increased while many workers continued to experience poverty and poor conditions.

👥 Luddites → workers who opposed machines they believed were destroying their jobs.

1811–1816 → Luddites attacked factories and destroyed labor-saving machinery in northern England.

📌 Industrialization created enormous wealth but distributed it unevenly.

title: 9.1.7 💰 Laissez-Faire and Free Market Economics
notes:
Laissez-faire → economic policy of limited government interference in business and free-market activity.

👤 Adam Smith → defended free-market economics in The Wealth of Nations (1776).

Three natural laws of economics:
• Self-interest → people work for their own benefit.
• Competition → competition encourages better products.
• Supply and demand → production and prices respond to market demand.

📌 Laissez-faire thinkers opposed strong government intervention in wages and working conditions.

title: 9.1.8 🔴 Socialism and Marxism
notes:
Socialism → economic system in which major factors of production are publicly owned and operated for social welfare.

Main goals → reduce poverty + increase equality + protect workers.

👤 Charles Fourier and Saint-Simon → early French socialist thinkers.

👤 Karl Marx + Friedrich Engels → developed Marxism.

📖 Communist Manifesto (1848) → presented Marx and Engels' major ideas.

🏦 Bourgeoisie → owners/control the means of production.
👷 Proletariat → working class that performs wage labor.

📌 Marxism → society is shaped by conflict between social classes.

title: 9.2 🇺🇸 THE AMERICAN WAR OF INDEPENDENCE
notes:
Background → Britain controlled 13 colonies in North America.

⚔️ Seven Years' War (1754–1763) → Britain defeated France but accumulated large debts.

Britain → expected American colonists to help pay war costs through taxation.

Colonists → opposed taxation without political representation.

🔑 Main issue → "taxation without representation".

📌 Enlightenment ideas → natural rights + social contract + right to resist unjust government influenced the colonial struggle.

title: 9.2.1 🧾 Causes of the American Revolution
notes:
Major causes →
• British taxation.
• Lack of colonial representation in Parliament.
• Defense of natural rights.
• Growing colonial self-government.
• Enlightenment political ideas.
• British attempts to control colonial trade and affairs.

📜 Stamp Act (1765) → required official stamps/taxes on wills, deeds, newspapers and other printed materials.

☕ Boston Tea Party (1773) → colonists dumped British tea into Boston Harbor to protest taxation and British policies.

📌 British punishment of Boston increased colonial resistance.

title: 9.2.2 ⚔️ Course of the American Revolution
notes:
1774 → First Continental Congress met in Philadelphia.

April 19, 1775 → fighting began at Lexington and Concord.

1775 → Second Continental Congress organized an army under 👤 George Washington.

July 4, 1776 → Declaration of Independence adopted.

👤 Thomas Jefferson → principal drafter of the Declaration.

📜 Declaration → based strongly on John Locke and Enlightenment ideas of natural rights and government by consent.

1778 → France entered the war against Britain.

1781 → British army under Lord Cornwallis surrendered at Yorktown.

🏆 Result → American independence.

title: 9.2.3 🏆 Effects of the American War of Independence
notes:
Major effects →
• Ended British colonial rule over the American colonies.
• Created an independent American nation.
• Contributed to the formation of the United States of America.
• Influenced the French Revolution.
• Influenced independence movements in Latin America.

⚠️ Limitation → slavery was not abolished by the revolution.

📌 American Revolution → important example of Enlightenment principles being used to challenge colonial rule.

title: 9.3 🇫🇷 THE FRENCH REVOLUTION
notes:
French Revolution → major political and social revolution beginning in 1789.

Old Regime (Ancien Régime) → absolute monarchy + unequal social structure + privileged estates.

🔑 Revolutionary ideals → liberty + equality + fraternity.

Main causes →
• Absolutism.
• Social inequality.
• Unfair taxation.
• Economic crisis and national bankruptcy.
• Poor harvests and famine.
• Mercantilist restrictions.
• Enlightenment ideas.
• Influence of the American Revolution.
• Political conflict over representation.

title: 9.3.1 👑 The Three Estates
notes:
French society was divided into three estates:

1️⃣ First Estate → high-ranking Catholic clergy; privileged.

2️⃣ Second Estate → nobility; privileged.

3️⃣ Third Estate → peasants + artisans + workers + bourgeoisie; majority of the population and heavily taxed.

📌 First + Second Estates → privileged and generally exempt from major taxes.
📌 Third Estate → carried much of the tax burden.

title: 9.3.2 💸 Economic and Intellectual Causes
notes:
Economic problems →
• Poor harvests.
• Food shortages.
• Rising hardship among peasants.
• Government bankruptcy.
• Heavy war expenditure.
• Deficit spending.
• Resistance of privileged groups to taxation.

🧠 Enlightenment influence → reason + natural rights + popular sovereignty + criticism of divine-right monarchy.

📌 French revolutionaries drew inspiration from earlier political revolutions and Enlightenment philosophers.

title: 9.3.3 🏛️ Estates-General and National Assembly
notes:
May 5, 1789 → Estates-General convened.

Problem → each estate had one vote, allowing the First and Second Estates to outvote the Third Estate.

Third Estate → demanded voting by population.

June 1789 → Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly.

🏟️ Tennis Court Oath → members promised to remain united until France had a written constitution.

June 23, 1789 → Louis XVI accepted the meeting of the three estates as a National Assembly and constitutional process began.

title: 9.3.4 🏰 Storming of the Bastille and Early Reforms
notes:
July 14, 1789 → people of Paris stormed the Bastille, a prison and symbol of royal despotism.

Effects → revolution spread across France; nobles were attacked; feudal records were destroyed; many nobles became émigrés.

October 5, 1789 → women marched to Versailles and forced the royal family to move to Paris.

Major reforms →
• Abolition of special privileges.
• Abolition of feudal dues.
• Equality before the law for men.
• Constitution of 1791.
• Declaration of the Rights of Man.
• Local-government reforms.
• Taxes based on ability to pay.

title: 9.3.5 📜 Declaration of the Rights of Man
notes:
Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen → expressed major revolutionary principles.

Key ideas →
• Liberty.
• Equality.
• Fraternity.
• Freedom of religion.
• Freedom of speech and press.
• Property rights.
• Fair trial.
• Right of people to make laws.

👩 Olympe de Gouges → demanded equal political rights for women through the Declaration of the Rights of Woman.

📌 Women gained some rights, including inheritance and easier divorce, but full political and social equality was not achieved.

title: 9.3.6 ⚖️ Constitution of 1791 and Legislative Assembly
notes:
1791 Constitution → created a limited monarchy.

Democratic features →
• King became head of state rather than absolute ruler.
• Legislative Assembly made laws.
• Feudalism abolished.

Undemocratic features →
• Voting limited mainly to taxpayers.
• Political offices restricted to property owners.

1791–1792 → Legislative Assembly period.

Political groups → Girondists + Jacobins.

📌 France moved from absolute monarchy toward constitutional government.

title: 9.3.7 ⚔️ Convention and the First French Republic
notes:
1792 → Convention replaced the Legislative Assembly.

September 22, 1792 → First French Republic established.

👥 Girondists → moderate political group associated with the wealthier middle class.

👥 Jacobins → more radical group associated with workers and popular revolutionary politics.

🌍 Foreign opposition → Austria + Prussia + Britain + Spain + Holland + Sardinia and other monarchies opposed revolutionary France.

👑 Louis XVI → tried for treason and executed by guillotine on January 21, 1793.

👑 Marie Antoinette → executed October 16, 1793.

title: 9.3.8 🩸 Reign of Terror
notes:
Reign of Terror → September 5, 1793 – July 27, 1794.

Purpose → suppress suspected enemies of the revolution and defend revolutionary France.

🏛️ Committee of Public Safety → powerful revolutionary body responsible for internal security and political repression.

👤 Georges Danton → major Jacobin leader; later executed.
👤 Maximilien Robespierre → became leading figure of the Committee of Public Safety.
👤 Jean-Paul Marat → important Jacobin revolutionary.

⚔️ Guillotine → execution machine known as the "National Razor".

📌 Approximately 15,000 people were executed by guillotine during the Terror according to the unit.

July 27–28, 1794 → Robespierre was overthrown and executed; Reign of Terror ended.

title: 9.3.9 🏛️ Directory and Results of the French Revolution
notes:
1795 → Constitution of Year III established the Directory.

Directory → five directors appointed by the legislature; lasted until 1799.

Problems → corruption + poor administration + economic hardship.

Important revolutionary achievements →
• Metric system adopted.
• Feudalism further weakened.
• Primogeniture abolished.
• Comprehensive legal system developed.
• Debt imprisonment ended.
• Slavery ended in French colonies during this revolutionary phase.
• Nationwide public education established.

📌 The revolution strengthened nationalism and spread ideas of citizenship, equality and constitutional government.

title: 9.4 👑 THE PERIOD OF NAPOLEON BONAPARTE
notes:
👤 Napoleon Bonaparte (1769–1821) → French military leader who rose to power after the Revolution.

December 25, 1799 → took power under the new constitution.

1799–1804 → Consulate period.

1804–1814 → Empire period.

December 2, 1804 → Napoleon crowned himself Emperor of France.

📌 Napoleon combined revolutionary reforms with centralized and authoritarian rule.

title: 9.4.1 ⚖️ Napoleon's Major Reforms
notes:
📜 Napoleonic Code → unified French law and protected private property.

Legal reforms →
• Equality before the law.
• Abolition of legal estates and privileges.
• Property rights.
• Secular government.
• Freedom of religion.
• Abolition of serfdom.

🏦 Bank of France (1800) → strengthened financial administration and public credit.

⛪ Concordat of 1801 → agreement with the Catholic Church; recognized freedom of worship and reorganized church-state relations.

🎓 Education → public education placed under state control.

🏛️ Administration → centralized and efficient bureaucracy.

📌 Napoleon preserved several important revolutionary achievements while limiting political freedom.

title: 9.4.2 ⚠️ Limitations of Napoleon's Rule
notes:
Major problems →
• Suppression of political opposition.
• Police surveillance.
• Restrictions on liberty.
• Workers could not freely form trade unions.
• Women had unequal legal status.
• Women remained legally dependent on husbands/fathers in many areas.
• Republican government was weakened.
• Absolutist tendencies increased.
• Nepotism → relatives placed on foreign thrones.
• Conquered peoples suffered from war and occupation.

📌 Napoleon's rule combined modernization with authoritarianism.

title: 9.4.3 ⚔️ Napoleon's Wars and Expansion
notes:
Napoleon fought major European powers including Britain, Austria, Prussia and Russia.

1805 → French and Spanish naval forces were defeated by Britain at the Battle of Trafalgar.

1807 → Treaty of Tilsit weakened Prussia and Russia and strengthened French influence.

1805 onward → Napoleon built a huge European empire.

🇩🇪 Confederation of the Rhine → Napoleon united 15 German states under French influence.

📌 Napoleon's military victories made France the dominant continental European power for a period.

title: 9.4.4 🚫 Continental System
notes:
Continental System → Napoleon's economic policy designed to weaken Britain by closing European ports to British commerce.

Goal → isolate Britain economically.

Problem → enforcement was difficult and the system damaged European trade.

1812 → American support for British commerce further weakened the system.

📌 The Continental System failed to destroy Britain's economic power.

title: 9.4.5 🇪🇸🇷🇺 Napoleon's Defeats
notes:
1808–1812 → Spanish resistance weakened French control in Spain.

1812 → Napoleon invaded Russia.

Russian campaign → disastrous losses weakened the French army.

1813 → coalition of Russia + Prussia + Austria + Britain defeated Napoleon at Leipzig, the Battle of Nations.

1814 → Allied forces entered Paris.

April 4, 1814 → Napoleon abdicated.

Louis XVIII → Bourbon monarchy restored.

May 30, 1814 → Treaty of Paris required France to surrender territories gained since 1792.

title: 9.4.6 🔥 The Hundred Days and Waterloo
notes:
1815 → Napoleon escaped from Elba and returned to France.

March–June 1815 → Hundred Days.

Napoleon → regained power and raised an army.

June 1815 → defeated at the Battle of Waterloo in Belgium by forces led by the Duke of Wellington and supported by Prussian troops.

After Waterloo → Napoleon was exiled to St. Helena in the South Atlantic.

1821 → Napoleon died on St. Helena.

📌 Waterloo → final defeat of Napoleon and end of his political rule.

title: 9.4.7 🏛️ Congress of Vienna, 1814–1815
notes:
Congress of Vienna → major European peace settlement held from September 1814 to June 1815.

Main goals →
• Restore political stability.
• Reorganize Europe's territories.
• Prevent another dominant European power.
• Restore traditional monarchies.

🇦🇹 Klemens von Metternich → Austrian statesman and major conservative force.
🇬🇧 Lord Castlereagh → represented Britain and supported balance of power.
🇷🇺 Alexander I → represented Russia.
🇫🇷 Talleyrand → represented France.
🇵🇷 Prussia → sought territorial compensation and expansion.

📌 Congress attempted to create a stable European political order after the Napoleonic Wars.

title: 9.4.8 ⚖️ Principles of the Congress of Vienna
notes:
Three major principles:

👑 Legitimacy → restore traditional ruling dynasties removed during revolutionary and Napoleonic wars.

🎁 Compensation → reward states that sacrificed resources and soldiers to defeat Napoleon.

⚖️ Balance of Power → arrange European territories so that no single state could dominate Europe and cause another general war.

📌 Examples → Bourbons restored in France, Spain and Naples; Britain gained strategic naval bases; Austria, Russia, Prussia and other powers received territorial compensation.
